newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai minister confirms central bank chief has quit.
newsitem.headline: Thai minister confirms central bank chief has quit.

text.p: A deputy minister in the Thai government confirmed on Tuesday that Bank of Thailand governor Rerngchai Marakanond has resigned from his post.
"I learnt from cabinet ministers that Rerngchai submitted his resignation yesterday," deputy minister of labour and social welfare Ekaporn Rakuamsak told Reuters.

The confirmation followed television reports late on Monday which quoted sources close to the governor as saying that he had submitted his resignation. Neither Rerngchai nor government officials were able to confirm the reports late on Monday.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh did not clearly acknowledge that the governor had quit when asked by reporters about the rumours late on Monday but said that he would make a statement on Tuesday.

The governor has in the past been the target of criticism for his handling of trouble in the ailing finance sector, and businesses have been frustrated by the central bank's decision to keep interest rates high despite a severe economic downturn.
The central bank's use of foreign reserves to stoutly defend the baht has also been criticised by some politicians and business leaders.
Rerngchai became governor of the central bank last July.
Some analysts speculated that among the front-runners to replace him as governor was the current deputy central bank governor, Chaiyawat Wibulsawasdi.
Rerngchai's resignation follows the controversial decision by the authorities to manage float the baht on July 2 and its subsequent plunge in value by over 20 percent.
Last week he launched a strong defence of the decision to float the baht.
His resignation also comes on the heels of a government decision to accept IMF advice on how to fix the Thai economy, which is going through its worst slump in over a decade.
Thailand is also studying whether or not to seek a standby credit line from the world body to help the country overcome current tight liquidity problems.
